record_identity.title: Singapore finance director transferred over US$499,000 after deepfake executive video call

incident_identity.date_basis: Date follows the reviewed registry or primary occurrence record; no narrower time is inferred.

summary: In March 2025, scammers contacted a multinational corporation’s finance director through WhatsApp, impersonating its chief financial officer. A purported lawyer stressed confidentiality and obtained a non-disclosure agreement. On 25 March the director joined a Zoom call with deepfake executive impersonators. Following the call and further messages, he transferred more than US$499,000 on 26 March to a local corporate mule account. Most of the funds then moved to Hong Kong. A request for another US$1.4 million prompted discovery on 27 March, and the director alerted HSBC. Singapore and Hong Kong police traced and withheld the Hong Kong proceeds on 28 March and seized the remaining local funds. The release did not establish when the money was returned to the company.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The Singapore Police Force’s 7 April 2025 release establishes the contact, deepfake call, transfer and cross-border response as a police-reported occurrence. It dates the initial contact to 24 March, call to 25 March, transfer to 26 March, discovery and bank alert to 27 March, and withholding to 28 March. The release reports a confidentiality demand and non-disclosure agreement from a purported lawyer. More than US$494,000 went to Hong Kong; more than US$5,000 remained locally and was seized. The additional US$1.4 million was requested, not reported as transferred. Withholding and seizure are not evidence of completed repayment. One reference to the originally scheduled meeting uses 2024 amid an otherwise March 2025 sequence; that inconsistent date is not used to reconstruct the actual call.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: Human scammers used deepfake video to impersonate senior company personnel during a live call and created false executive authority for a transfer exceeding US$499,000. Police evidence establishes the transfer and later withholding and seizure, not completed repayment. The scam objective belongs to the human operators, not the synthetic media system. The synthetic executive solicitation and consequential deception failures remain bounded to the reported transfer. Later police withholding mitigates loss without making the original disclosure/transfer authorised. The OECD AI-awareness proposition is Not aligned in the deceptive interaction; no binding duty is asserted.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: High-value payment controls must authenticate the transaction and the authority behind it through an independent channel, not only the apparent face and voice of senior personnel. Recovery after transfer is valuable but cannot substitute for approval procedures resilient to real-time impersonation.
assessment_boundaries: The record relies on the reported police account and does not identify the victim company or every participant in the call.
The evidence does not establish which tools or models produced the synthetic media.
More than US$499,000 was transferred before police traced and withheld the funds; ultimate unrecovered loss is not asserted.
The occurrence does not establish negligence or legal liability by the victim or service providers.

clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: An executed transfer and subsequent fund movement are distinct from the preceding solicitation.

clauses.source_paraphrase: A further request for US$1.4 million on 27 March prompted discovery. The director alerted HSBC, which notified Singapore’s Anti-Scam Centre.

clauses.source_paraphrase: On 28 March, Hong Kong police withheld the amount transferred there, and Singapore police seized more than US$5,000 remaining locally. The police release described an ongoing investigation.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Withholding and seizure mitigate loss but do not establish the date funds were returned to the victim.

external_requirement_assessments.assessment_basis: The AI-mediated executive video directly engages stakeholder awareness of interaction with AI. The police account describes real executives being impersonated to induce the transfer, with the victim discovering the scam later. Meaningful awareness was withheld in that interaction; this independently contradicts Section 1.3(ii), irrespective of voluntary status.

The synthetic executive video was presented as a genuine executive interaction before the victim transferred funds. The police account establishes later discovery rather than advance disclosure. The specific NIST requirement to document GAI interaction to the user before interactive activity therefore did not hold in this bounded interaction; organisational framework adoption is not required.
